summary: Every region of Japan claims a signature dish. Tokyo alone has enough to fill a trip — but the twelve below are the ones worth getting right. Try them at a specialist, not a generalist.

dishes.name: Sushi
dishes.origin: Edomae-zushi (modern hand-formed nigiri) was invented in Edo (now Tokyo) in the early 1800s.
dishes.made_of: Vinegared short-grain rice topped with raw fish, seafood, or egg. Soy sauce and wasabi accompany — never mix them.
dishes.vegan_notes: Inari (tofu-pouch) and kappa-maki (cucumber) are reliably vegan.
dishes.must_try_form: Omakase at a counter — the chef picks your progression.

dishes.name: Ramen
dishes.origin: Arrived from China in the late 1800s; each Japanese region later evolved its own broth style.
dishes.made_of: Wheat noodles in broth (tonkotsu pork, shoyu soy, miso, or shio salt) with toppings — chashu, egg, menma, nori.
dishes.vegan_notes: Hard to find — most broths use pork or fish. T's Tantan and Afuri have proper vegan bowls.
dishes.must_try_form: Tonkotsu at a specialist. Don't linger — ramen is meant to be eaten in under 15 minutes.

dishes.name: Tempura
dishes.origin: Portuguese missionaries introduced fritter-style cooking in the 16th century; Japan refined it into tempura.
dishes.made_of: Seafood and vegetables in an ice-cold, lightly beaten batter, flash-fried in shallow oil. Served with dashi-based tentsuyu sauce or salt.
dishes.vegan_notes: Yasai tempura (vegetable-only) is a standard option at most tempura counters.
dishes.must_try_form: Counter omakase at a Michelin-star tempura specialist like Tempura Kondo.

dishes.name: Tonkatsu
dishes.origin: 19th-century Japan adapted Western schnitzel into the panko-crusted cutlet we know today.
dishes.made_of: Thick pork cutlet — loin (rōsu) or fillet (hire) — breaded in coarse panko and deep-fried. Served with shredded cabbage, rice, and tangy tonkatsu sauce.
dishes.must_try_form: Kurobuta (Berkshire pork) at a specialist; the meat pinks up even through a full fry.

dishes.name: Yakitori
dishes.origin: Charcoal-grilled skewers are an Edo-era izakaya staple.
dishes.made_of: Bite-sized chicken — thigh, breast, liver, skin, cartilage, or tsukune meatballs — grilled over binchōtan charcoal with salt or tare soy glaze.
dishes.vegan_notes: Many yakitori spots also grill vegetable skewers (yakimono) — shishito peppers, shiitake, asparagus.
dishes.must_try_form: Omakase at a smoky counter. Don't sauce the skin skewer — salt-only is sacrilege otherwise.

dishes.name: Okonomiyaki
dishes.origin: Osaka and Hiroshima claim rival styles; both emerged in post-war Japan.
dishes.made_of: A batter of flour, egg, dashi, and shredded cabbage, mixed with your choice of pork belly, seafood, or cheese; griddled and topped with okonomiyaki sauce, mayo, aonori seaweed, and bonito flakes.
dishes.vegan_notes: Vegan okonomiyaki exists at specialist diners; skip the bonito flakes and request dashi-free batter.
dishes.must_try_form: Cook-it-yourself on a teppan at a specialist in Shinjuku or Tsukishima (Monja Street).

dishes.name: Takoyaki
dishes.made_of: Ball-shaped savoury pancakes filled with octopus, green onion, and pickled ginger, cooked in a special dimpled cast-iron pan.
dishes.must_try_form: Straight off the pan at a stall — they're dangerously hot for the first minute.

dishes.name: Soba
dishes.origin: Edo-era staple; Tokyo's water is still said to make the best soba noodles.
dishes.made_of: Buckwheat noodles, served cold with dipping sauce (zaru soba) or in a hot broth (kake soba). 100% buckwheat (jūwari) is gluten-free; 80/20 blend (nihachi) is not.
dishes.vegan_notes: The dipping sauce usually contains dashi — ask for shōjin (vegan-style) dashi or plain soy.
dishes.must_try_form: Cold zaru soba on a hot day, at a stand-up shop inside a major station.

dishes.name: Udon
dishes.origin: Regional pride centres on Kagawa prefecture (Sanuki udon), but Tokyo has strong versions.
dishes.made_of: Thick, chewy wheat flour noodles served hot in kake broth, cold with dipping sauce, or in hearty nabeyaki hot pots.
dishes.vegan_notes: Sanuki udon with plain kake broth and tempura vegetables is one of the easier vegan options.
dishes.must_try_form: Bukkake udon with ginger, scallion, and grated daikon on top.

dishes.name: Kaiseki
dishes.origin: Evolved from the tea ceremony in Kyoto in the 16th century.
dishes.made_of: A multi-course tasting menu with strict seasonality — usually 8-14 tiny courses, each on hand-picked ceramic ware, progressing through raw, boiled, grilled, steamed, and rice courses.
dishes.vegan_notes: Shōjin ryōri (temple vegan kaiseki) is the historical root; modern kaiseki restaurants will accommodate if you book ahead.
dishes.must_try_form: Reserve 30+ days ahead at a ryokan or a specialist restaurant.

dishes.name: Wagyu
dishes.origin: Four Japanese cattle breeds, with Kobe, Matsusaka, Ōmi, and Hida beef as the prestige regional grades.
dishes.made_of: Marbled beef from Japanese native breeds, graded A1-A5 for fat quality. The intramuscular fat melts at body temperature, which is why you see the 'melts in the mouth' cliché.
dishes.must_try_form: Teppanyaki counter (chef cooks in front of you) or yakiniku (grill-at-the-table).

dishes.name: Matcha
dishes.origin: Arrived from China in the 12th century; the Japanese tea ceremony (chanoyu) shaped what matcha became.
dishes.made_of: Shade-grown green tea leaves stone-ground into a fine powder. Whisked with hot water in a chawan bowl to froth — never steeped.
similar_to: No direct equivalent — most green teas are steeped leaves, not powder.
dishes.vegan_notes: Inherently vegan. Matcha lattes at many Tokyo cafés now offer soy / oat milk.
dishes.must_try_form: Ceremonial-grade usucha at a tea room — sit seiza, receive the bowl with both hands, rotate twice, and drink in three sips.
